title: The difficult
hookLine: love isn't only for the easy ones

lines: BEGIN THE MORNING BY SAYING TO THYSELF.
cards: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial."
That's how a Roman emperor, Marcus Aurelius, opens the second book of his private notebook. Not a pep talk. A weather report.
He ran an empire, and he knew the day would include people who were hard to be around.
So do the rest of us: a coworker who takes credit, a relative who knows exactly which button to press, a neighbor with a leaf blower and opinions. Loving the easy ones takes no training at all.

teach.b: First, the emperor's warning. Marcus goes on: these people act as they do because they don't know what is good and bad.
None of them can make him do wrong, so none of them can really injure him, and he can't hate them, because they are his kin.
Then, surprising for an emperor: we are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids. To work against each other is against nature.

Second, bread for an enemy. The book of Proverbs puts it in kitchen terms: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." Nothing about warm feelings.
Bread and water, handed to someone who wishes you harm.

Third, the hard one comes last. In the Path of Purification, the Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa gives an order for loving-kindness practice: yourself, then a dear friend, then someone neutral, and only then someone hostile.
He warns against starting with the hostile person, because resentment comes up first. He doesn't pretend it's easy; he builds a ramp.
Fourth, well-wishing isn't trusting. None of these voices asks anyone to hand a difficult person the car keys.
Wishing someone well can sit alongside a locked door, a firm no, a boundary kept: hoping they find their way to being well, from a safe distance if need be.
The hard ones too. Not first, not instead of safety, but too.

how: In Buddhist loving-kindness practice, people often wish well to themselves, a friend and a neutral person before turning to someone difficult; Jews and Christians read Proverbs 25 on feeding a hungry enemy as practical guidance; Stoics prepare in the morning for the people they will meet.

o: people you must trust again once you forgive them
strangers you've never had any reason to love
the people who are hard to love, wished well anyway

games.q: who said what about the hard ones — tap the pairs.
p: bread and water for an enemy

s: Buddhaghosa says to begin loving-kindness with your enemy
he starts with yourself and warns against starting with a hostile person.
Marcus Aurelius said we are made for cooperation, like hands and feet
he says working against each other is against nature.
wishing a difficult person well means you have to trust them again
wishing someone well can sit alongside a firm boundary.

games.q: you're starting loving-kindness practice for the first time. where do you begin?
o: with the person who hurt you most.
games.why: Buddhaghosa's order starts with yourself, then a dear friend, then someone neutral, and the hostile person last.

practice: Walk Buddhaghosa's ramp slowly: may I be well, then a friend for a few breaths, then a neutral face from the store, and only then someone mildly difficult, a person who simply irritates you, offered the same wish.
If resentment comes up, go back to the friend for a breath and try again. If you pray, you can name them before God.

wordCard.voice: The difficult. The people who are hard to love, whom Marcus expected each morning, Proverbs says to feed anyway, and Buddhaghosa placed last on the ramp. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the hard ones too. Bread and water count, even when the warmth is missing. See you tomorrow.
